response:
Evidence, mostly. If a question can be settled by looking at the world, I want to look, and I trust a good dataset over an elegant argument. Clever reasoning has a long history of arriving confidently at wrong conclusions, and intuition is worst exactly where it feels most certain.

That said, I don't think the two are really rivals. Data doesn't interpret itself. Deciding what counts as evidence, what a study actually shows, or whether a measurement captures the thing you care about is all philosophical work. And plenty of questions I find most interesting, like what makes a life go well or what we owe each other, can't be settled by data alone. There, careful reasoning is the only tool available, and I enjoy that kind of thinking a lot.

On intuition, I treat it as a signal to investigate, not a verdict. If an argument leads somewhere that feels deeply wrong, I take that as a reason to recheck the premises, but sometimes the intuition is the thing that has to give.

So my inclination is empirical first, with philosophy doing the work of keeping the empiricism honest. Where do you fall? I'm curious whether you asked because you lean the other way.
